title: Elevated serum interferon-α2 associates with activity and flare risk in juvenile-onset systemic lupus erythematosus

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: jSLE active/intermediate disease activity vs. Low Disease Activity State (LDAS)
jSLE active/intermediate disease activity vs. remission sub-group
All jSLE patients vs. Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) patients
All jSLE patients vs. Healthy Controls (HCs)
jSLE patients in remission or LDAS with abnormal IFN-α2 levels (predicting time to flare within 6 months)
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Median 91 days to flare (abnormal IFN-α2) vs. 128 days (normal IFN-α2), P = 0.022 (cross-sectional). Hazard Ratio 2.1 (95% CI 1.0–4.2, P = 0.041) (longitudinal).

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Detecting an ongoing disease flare in jSLE
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Odds Ratio 3.84 (95% CI 1.15–12.80), P = 0.028 (multivariable longitudinal analysis)

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Predicting subsequent disease flares in jSLE (univariable analysis)

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Juvenile Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (jSLE) disease activity and flare occurrence
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Elevated IFN-α2 levels in jSLE are linked to its established role in SLE pathogenesis. This involves a complex interplay of genetic contributors (e.g., variants affecting cytoplasmic nucleic acid clearance or enhancing cytoplasmic acid sensor activation) and immune responses to tissue damage (e.g., infections, ultraviolet radiation, mechanical stress). These stimuli lead to accumulation of cellular debris and nuclear material, activating TLR3/7 pathways, and ultimately driving IFN production. Increased genetic burden in pediatric populations may contribute to more pronounced IFN expression and a more severe clinical phenotype in jSLE.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: IFN-α2 levels showed a clear relationship with disease activity intensity: higher levels (median 3185 fg/ml) were observed in active/intermediate jSLE compared to LDAS (571 fg/ml, P=0.04) and remission (271 fg/ml, P<0.001), indicating a 'dose-response' effect with disease severity. No significant association was found between IFN-α2 levels and prednisolone treatment dosage, suggesting limited influence of glucocorticoids on the type I IFN pathway.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: IFN-α2 levels were significantly higher in jSLE patients compared to JIA patients and Healthy Controls, indicating specificity to jSLE rather than general inflammation. Ethnically, patients of Black African/Caribbean descent showed higher median serum IFN-α2 levels (1326 fg/ml) compared to White individuals (134 fg/ml, P=0.028), regardless of disease activity, suggesting ethnic specificity. No significant differences were found based on sex. IFN-α2 was the only biomarker among those tested (including anti-dsDNA antibodies, C3, and ESR) that significantly predicted an ongoing flare in multivariable longitudinal analysis.

clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Quantification of serum IFN-α2 levels is associated with disease activity and can predict ongoing and future flares in jSLE. Elevated IFN-α2 levels are indicative of higher disease activity and a significantly shorter time to disease flares (within 6 months), suggesting its utility for risk stratification and disease monitoring in this patient group.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Adverse risk. Higher IFN-α2 levels signify increased disease activity and a heightened risk of experiencing disease flares, which represents an adverse health outcome for jSLE patients.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The Simoa digital immunoassay for IFN-α2 is characterized by high sensitivity, specificity, and cost-effectiveness for large-scale studies. However, limitations include relatively high variation in 23% of experimental duplicates, especially near the lower limit of detection. Potential interference from anti-IFN-α2 auto-antibodies (present in up to a quarter of SLE patients), issues with antibody specificity, cross-reactivity, standardization, and dynamic range limitations were also noted. The authors conclude that 'additional work is required to further improve IFN-α2 quantification prior to its introduction into clinical practice'.
